A novel approach to acquiring and aligning four-dimensional MRI images, encompassing three dimensions plus respiratory data, without requiring breath-holding, is presented. This method utilizes a modified, high-speed 2D spin-echo sequence and demonstrates superior motion resistance compared to conventional gradient-echo techniques. The technique employs a large number of rapidly collected images, allowing for free-breathing scans with narrow, narrow bandwidths. A motion-compensation framework, consisting of an optimized multi-segment echo train and post-collection realignment, is used to achieve this. The results, obtained through a high-resolution, four-dimensional T2-weighted dataset, are suitable for various clinical purposes, such as surgical planning, target identification, and reference for real-time, motion-guided imaging. The efficacy of this method is shown through applications in image quality, quantitative MRI, and guiding real-time imaging with an electrocardiogram.

The exact paired-permutation test, a nonparametric inference method for
dependent, potentially non-i.i.d. data, relies on a test statistic that is
invariant under paired-data permutations within its application range. As a
general rule, pre-computing the exact distribution of the test statistic under
all possible paired-data permutations becomes computationally prohibitive for
statistic and dataset sizes commonly encountered in machine learning. In this
work, we introduce an accelerated, rejection-control-based paired-test
framework that streamlines non-i.i.d. test statistic evaluation within the
paired-permutation testing range. Our method's efficiency hinges on a Monte
Carlo estimate of the tail probability and a subsequent control of the rejection
rate under a hyper-rectangle encompassing the test statistic. This approach
enables paired-permutation tests with test dimensions in the order of $100$ for
data sets containing $10^5$ instances and includes machine learning models as
testable objects for paired-data stability evaluation. Our method is made
available as an open-source, paired-permutation test library in Python.

A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping quantities, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrap prices for global cargo vessels is presented, spanning the years 1966 to 2019 and covering 44,130 monthly observations. This dataset was assembled to support research into the freight market. We have compiled monthly average freight rates from leading industry publications, along with data on new, used, and scrap ship prices and shipping quantities from respected industry sources. Although these records are widely accessible, their fragmented nature limits their usefulness in time series analysis that requires access to a broad spectrum of related variables. This dataset is not intended to substitute for existing datasets on new and used ship prices, which have been compiled over recent decades by renowned researchers in the field. Rather, it is designed to facilitate research by providing seamless access to major industry statistics, including new and used ship prices, which have been consistently recorded and categorized throughout the timeframe.

We define loom spaces as a more general framework that includes both surface spaces and pseudosurface spaces. Through this framework, we define veering triangulations for loom spaces in a way that extends the veering triangulations previously defined for pseudosurfaces. We then identify specific properties of veering triangulations on loom spaces that mirror those found for veering triangulations on pseudosurfaces.

This research focuses on developing an automated approach to forecast stock prices for Samsung Electronics, utilizing natural language processing and machine learning techniques. Initially, we employ a BERT-based sentiment analysis model to extract features from news articles related to the company. To address class imbalance in the data, we incorporate these features into a support vector machine for price prediction. Further improvements are made by utilizing a generative adversarial network to generate additional training data. Our results demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing models, achieving higher accuracy, precision, recall, and an adjusted F1 score of 0.94, 0.94, 0.94, and 0.94, respectively.

An in-depth investigation of double Higgs boson production in $e^+e^+$ colliders, specifically the ILC and CLIC, has been conducted for various theories, including the Standard Model, Two-Higgs-Doublet Model, and Standard Model Extension. A systematic study was carried out for different theories and configurations of ILC and CLIC, taking into account detector effects. By analyzing the final states resulting from top quark pair decay, the study found that the ILC1000 configuration offers the highest discovery potential for exotic Higgs boson couplings, with up to 95% efficiency for the MSSM and 90% efficiency for the SM EFT. On the other hand, the CLIC3000 configuration offers a broader coverage of the parameter space, with up to 95% efficiency for the MSSM and 90% efficiency for the SM EFT. Notably, the ILC3000 configuration offers a broader coverage of the parameter space compared to the ILC1000 configuration, with a 90% efficiency for the MSSM and 70% efficiency for the SM EFT.

We perform a covariant expansion of the Einstein-Hilbert action in powers of
$1/c^2$, considering a general spacetime foliation defined by $c$, the speed
of light. We achieve this through the application of a suitable 'pre-non-
relativistic' geometrical formalism, which enables us to derive the Einstein-
 Hilbert action's $c$ expansion to a second non-relativistic traceless
 Lagrangian density with remarkable efficiency and generality. This method
 allows us to derive a non-relativistic gravity theory framework from a
 purely geometric perspective, which is then foliated into three dimensions
 and two dimensions.

We investigated the drag coefficients of long cylindrical shapes moving through a granular layer, considering both flat-bottomed and V-shaped grooved bases, as they moved through a layer of glass beads, glass spheres, and mixtures of the two. We found that the resistance experienced by the cylinders varied significantly depending on the type of ground material, the shape of the base, and the cylinders' orientation. Specifically, the base shape had a greater effect on drag than the cylinders' orientation. The best way to predict the resistance these cylinders experienced was using a modified version of the 2D drag equation, taking into account the flow patterns created around the cylinders. Our research also showed that the resistance experienced by the cylinders was influenced by the grain size, depth of the ground, and the shape of the bottom, with the flat-bottomed design generally experiencing the highest resistance.

Our research utilized the multiphase transport (AMPT) model to examine the relationship between particle transverse momentum and triangular flow in the mid-rapidity region at top energy. To enhance the model's accuracy in simulating initial charge fluctuations, we modified it to include gluon triangular flow and correlated quark correlations. We found that at top energy, particles with low momentum exhibit a positive correlation with triangular symmetry in both Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions, but this correlation decreases for higher momentum. Additionally, we discovered that initial geometric and flow fluctuations significantly impact particle flow in the mid-rapidity region. We also observed that the AMPT model with modified initial conditions can effectively explain the differences between the predictions made by hydrodynamics and the experimental data.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas: neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as rare electroweak processes occurring at a rare rate. Specifically, researchers have examined the occurrence of $B^0_s$ to muon-antimuon decay, initially searching for new physics beyond the Standard Model. They also investigated various $B^0_s$ decay processes involving charmless down-type or strange-type quarks, utilizing the high event selection capability of the ATLAS detector. All measurements were made with reference to those predicted by the Standard Model, with the goal of uncovering indications of new physics, particularly in rare $B^0_s$ decays. In one instance, scientists studied $B^0_s$ to $J/\psi K^0_S$ mixing-induced CP violation for the first time, and in another, they measured the branching fraction of the rare process $B^0_s$ to $D^0 \gamma$ for the first time.

A new class of numerical methods, specifically semi-discretisations, has been developed to preserve key physical properties when solving time-dependent partial differential equations. These methods achieve this by utilizing symplectic integrators, resulting in a discretised system with a linear system that has a Hermitian positive definite matrix and a skew-Hermitian matrix. This system is complex and challenging to solve efficiently using iterative preconditioned Krylov subspace methods, particularly when dealing with large-scale problems. To address this challenge, we have developed a new type of preconditioner that leverages the structural features of the system matrix and takes advantage of a widely-used thermodynamic operator as a proxy. This new approach enables the use of an existing, efficient preconditioner for the symplectic part of the system, leading to improved scalability when combined with parallel computing and domain decomposition techniques. Our results demonstrate the scalability of this method when used in conjunction with this type of preconditioner.

Soft-tissue registration is a complex task due to significant inter-patient variations and noise in medical images. Our research focuses on developing a soft-tissue volume-to-surface registration method that leverages a computationally efficient, patient-specific biomechanical model. This novel framework combines a mass-spring system with a finite element model to ensure physically realistic results. To make the model more manageable, we made several assumptions to reduce computational demands and model complexity. Our approach uses an optimized spring constant to match the target surface with the model, resulting in a robust and efficient registration method. To test our method, we conducted experiments on both synthetic data and real MRI images of the heart and liver, comparing our results with other state-of-the-art methods. Our findings demonstrate that our approach outperforms competing techniques in terms of accuracy and performance.

Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories of objects and surfaces within a three-dimensional animation sequence.  Adversarial Self-Supervised 3D Scene Flow Estimation has been widely used to obtain robust scene flow models against errors in 3D reconstruction data.  Most existing methods construct a neighbor graph based on the similarity of flow patterns to generate adversarial samples for training.  However, we discovered that this approach can be misleading, as it may confuse target points with already correctly estimated flow patterns rather than truly robust ones.  To address this issue, we propose a novel strategy for identifying reliable neighbor structures by leveraging the consistency of depth maps. This approach leverages the fact that corresponding flow patterns should result in the same destination map, thereby providing a geometrically consistent reference for finding neighboring samples. This approach is universally applicable to various self-supervised scene flow algorithms and does not necessitate a complex 3D reconstruction process. We evaluate our method on the large-scale Shape2Flow dataset, achieving state-of-the-art results and outperforming other leading Adversarial Self-Supervised approaches in multiple domain-specific benchmarks.

In recent years, AI systems with deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success in various tasks. However, these approaches often require substantial computational resources and produce high levels of computational waste. In natural environments where information is limited, this inefficiency can be particularly limiting. To overcome these challenges, researchers have turned to the spiking neural network paradigm, which emulates the biological neural system and utilizes binary spikes for computation. While promising, the potential of RSNs has not yet been fully realized due to the complexity of training deep RSNs. In this study, we introduce a simple RSN structure and employ random initialization to initialize the weights of a large network, which is then fine-tuned using a smaller, randomly initialized network as an initializer. Experimental results on image classification tasks with the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets show that this approach leads to an order of magnitude speedup in inference time and up to three times lower energy consumption compared to traditional RSN methods.

This research investigates the thermodynamic properties of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, using the MIT bag model. By employing the path integral formalism, we derived the grand canonical density for both polarized up and down quarks, considering their quark chemical potentials. Furthermore, we used the grand canonical densities to develop the equations of state for polarized spin up and down quarks within the framework of the MIT bag model. These equations were then utilized to determine the structure of spin-polarized strange quark matter through the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equation in the presence of a strong magnetic field. The resulting model's predictions were visually represented through radial profiles of energy density, pressure, and pressure anisotropy, as well as temperature-baryon chemical potential phase diagrams and magnetization-baryon chemical phase diagrams. The research also highlighted the impact of the external magnetic field on the strange star's radius and its relationship with the star's spin polarization.

A perfect matching in a graph is a set of edges that covers all vertices, and whose edges do not share any vertices. A cubic graph has the property that a perfect matching can be removed to yield a 2-factor, which is a collection of cycles that also covers all vertices. In this work, we investigate the number of perfect matchings and Hamiltonian cycles in a specific class of cubic graphs denoted as G(n,m). These graphs G(n,m) are derived from the toroidal grid by adding diagonals to a (2n x 2m) lattice, and have at most (4nm/3)+1 perfect matchings. Notably, for a specific subset of graph parameters, the number of perfect matchings is precisely (4nm/3). These matchings, when coloured, result in graphs with uniquely edge-coloured 2-cycles, and we find that the number of such graphs with uniquely coloured 2-cycles is exactly as many as the number of partitions of nm into even parts.

This paper introduces a novel approach called Timeloops, a reinforcement learning algorithm designed to automate the configuration of containerized container orchestration systems for containerized microservices. As the number of possible system settings increases, traditional trial-and-error methods fail to efficiently determine optimal parameters. Timeloops addresses this challenge by employing reinforcement learning to guide the exploration of system settings and a value function to evaluate the worth of particular configurations. A heuristic strategy is utilized to select a diverse range of configurations for thorough testing, while the evaluation of configurations is carried out through value iteration on a Markov decision process. The efficacy of Timeloops is demonstrated through testing on both simple and complex system settings for the Quake game, showcasing significant performance improvements over random exploration.

This study develops a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter where target appearance probabilities are organized on a grid, and individual grid cell probabilities are calculated and discarded as necessary. The method is particularly useful in sensor management applications, where the decision to deploy sensors is based on whether targets are present in a specific area. The filter is further optimized by eliminating unoccupied grid cells from the state, significantly reducing memory usage and computational costs. A real-time wildlife tracking example is used to illustrate the filter's effectiveness.

This study examines the null controllability of a population model that includes an interior degenerate diffusion component. By first establishing a new Carleman estimate for the adjoint system in its entirety, we then deduce observability inequalities necessary to prove the null controllability of the population dynamics in the absence and presence of a reaction term. Consequently, through Nirenberg's implicit function theorem applied to these inequalities, we derive the existence of steering time and control norm lower bounds.

The effectiveness of soccer players in making split-second decisions can significantly influence the outcome of matches. In this study, we investigated this aspect using soccer data from the 2018-2019 Serie A season in Italy, focusing on pivotal moments that could lead to scoring opportunities for both teams. We analyzed over 2,400 situations for each team, examining the impact of an ideal decision on each team's chances of advancing, then developed a model to predict decisions made by players and another to evaluate their suitability. Notably, our model's assessments of decision quality were highly accurate when compared to actual data. Furthermore, a reinforcement learning approach was employed to optimize decision-making, with the learned policy showing superior performance to real players in various scenarios. However, the study also revealed that the average impact of individual decisions on soccer games is minimal, typically affecting probabilities by less than 10%.

High-resolution subsurface imaging through seismic waveform inversion (DWI) is a highly effective method. High-resolution subsurface imaging through seismic waveform inversion (DWI) is an effective method to achieve high-resolution subsurface imaging. The two current DWI approaches utilize waveforms at the sensor locations as input, and source information in DWI can provide additional constraints for more precise imaging. WS-WFI combines waveform and extended source information, but it has limitations due to its reliance on accurate source information and its inability to handle misregistration between sensor data and modeling. TWSWI, our novel framework, overcomes these challenges by employing a multi-task learning strategy with an attention mechanism, enabling accurate and robust DWI even with imperfect source information. TWSWI treats full-waveform data as one task and simulated source information as multiple tasks, and through an attention mechanism, it dynamically adjusts the importance of each task during optimization. Numerical experiments demonstrate the superior performance of TWSWI in terms of improved imaging quality and reduced loss compared to current DWI methods.

An extended stochastic spatial model of two species interacting on a 2D lattice incorporates local interactions within an environment subject to random fluctuations. The model includes a scenario where species compete locally through overtopping when conditions are favorable, and species can also colonize distant areas under certain conditions. The dynamics of this situation were previously studied in a noise-free setting, where it was found that one species would dominate depending on which trait gave it an advantage. The species that can only interact locally would win in the absence of noise, while the species that can colonize distant areas would win in highly noisy settings. Our research reveals that species that coexist can emerge when noise is introduced, a phenomenon facilitated by random fluctuations that allow two populations with no stable coexistence to suddenly interact and protect one another. It was found that an intermediate level of noise results in one species dominating, whereas both species would be lost at very low or very high noise levels. This result is in direct contrast to the stochastic version of the competition-colonization tradeoff model that is based on a lottery, where only the species that can colonize distant areas would win in the presence of noise.

This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network that utilizes intelligent reflecting surfaces to support nearby device-to-device communication. The goal is to maximize the total data transmitted while ensuring a minimum level of power generated and keeping the nearby D2D signal interference within acceptable limits. Initially, a problem is formulated to determine the optimal settings for the diagonal phase shifts and digital beamforming that can be jointly adjusted. To tackle the resulting complex, non-convex problem, a joint convex optimization method is applied after transforming parts of the variable space. Subsequently, a partial optimization of the feeding network is carried out using convex relaxation and randomization techniques. The proposed algorithm is shown to effectively address the integrated data and energy networking problem with minimal loss. Numerical results highlight the ability of the designed surface to significantly boost performance in integrated data and energy transmission networks.

The surge in teleworking necessitated the adaptation of laboratory systems to
allow for remote operation. This document presents the specifics of operating
an LDV system to perform velocity field measurements without physical presence,
with the goal of acquiring two-dimensional data. The procedure entails several
phases, including acquiring planar measurements at a single location and at
several locations to construct a 2D field, two methods of which are presented.

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates in TEM is examined, with emphasis on their potential to counteract spherical aberration. Our analysis of their design reveals inherent limitations, particularly their inability to correct spherical aberration due to their fixed, plate-like structure. However, we explore the possibility of a novel design that could correct lower-order spherical aberration by incorporating a radial phase gradient. This enhanced model is used to simulate its impact on TEM images. We then compare its performance to both conventional phase plates and uncorrected spherical aberration. The results highlight the limitations of static programmable phase plates in correcting spherical aberration but also suggest that real-time programmable phase plates could offer significant benefits in specific applications.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state.

We derive new conclusions regarding the additive Galois module properties of specific wildly ramified finite non-abelian extensions of Q. Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with a Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we determine essential and sufficient conditions for the ring of integers in K to be freely generated over its associated order within the rational group ring constructed from the Galois group G.

In experiments conducted at Belle II, an search has been initiated on axion-like particles generated in the decay of $B$ mesons, specifically the $B^0 \to \bar{d} \gamma$ process. A two-step analysis is employed to first identify $B$ mesons and then identify events where the second decay product is either undetected or occurs outside the standard detector range. Utilizing this method, stringent limits have been established on axion interaction parameters, surpassing previous achievements by a factor of 2 to 4. In addition, an alternative analysis is proposed where the second decay product is required to be an electron, allowing for exploration of certain rare decay modes with significantly enhanced sensitivity.

This study provides a detailed examination of the potential pitfalls in using
contextualized language models for monitoring semantic shifts in words. In our
analysis, we employed BERT to detect the direction of the shift of a large
number of words across various time periods and languages, revealing both
successful cases and periods where BERT misjudged the true direction of
change. In investigating 50 instances of BERT making erroneous predictions, we
found numerous instances where BERT's evaluations were influenced by
stereotypes, political biases, or shifts in word meanings unrelated to
social dynamics. In contrast, we found BERT to be reliable in detecting
shifts related to technological advancements. In discussing the limitations
of contextual language models, we found BERT to excel in cases where
changes in societal values drove shifts in the connotations of words.

If a heavy quasar is in a state of superradiance, it becomes the source of a dense cloud made up of particles of a specific type of extremely light boson, which fills and eventually leaves the space around the black hole. By measuring the frequency at which these particles orbit the space around the black hole, scientists can calculate the mass of these extremely light bosons. By comparing frequencies of particles around black hole systems with different spin rates, researchers can confirm if they are caused by the same type of extremely light boson or different ones. This method allows for setting upper limits on how common specific types of extremely light bosons can be. Moreover, if any of these dense clouds of particles of specific extremely light bosons can interact with each other, scientists can use this fact to set limits on how these interactions occur.

A crucial stage in neural tissue development involves the oscillation of nuclear positions between the ventricular and subventricular zones, a behavior known as interkinetic nuclear migration (INM). This phenomenon was observed in zebrafish retinas, and our study presents a novel perspective on the dynamics of nuclear migration. By tracking individual nuclei through live imaging, we discovered that INM results from the collective movement of nuclei through tissue diffusion, rather than distinct phases observed previously. This understanding is supported by mathematical modeling and computational simulations, which replicate the observed dynamics. Furthermore, we propose a mathematical framework that accounts for the non-random movement of nuclei, and our analysis reveals that this behavior varies among different species and developmental stages.

In image processing tasks like color image demosaicing and video compressed sensing, image reconstruction from incomplete data is a critical issue. In these scenarios, accurate reconstruction relies heavily on the sparsity of transformed images, a property that is typically assumed but not guaranteed. A more reliable approach is to design codes that ensure image sparsity in a specific transform domain, a concept explored in this paper. The research focuses on two distinct applications, sharing the same underlying problem of minimizing the code's impact on perceived image quality while ensuring sparsity in a specific transform domain. A novel optimization framework is developed, a gradient-based method is devised to solve this complex problem, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through improved reconstruction quality in both test cases, significantly enhancing code's utility in image processing applications.

We've developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory to describe the collective behavior of polar particles in complex, variable environments. This model takes into account the variations in particle number and model parameters across different spatial areas. Using both small perturbation techniques and large-scale simulations, we've analyzed the movement of these particles in environments with randomly scattered obstacles. When the density of these particles is low and they're moving in two-dimensional spaces, we found that they move in a rhythmic pattern, with their speed depending on how many of them there are, how much they propel themselves, and the viscous forces acting upon them. This behavior differs significantly from that of particles that don't move in response to currents. As the number of particles increases, their movement becomes more synchronized, and this is especially pronounced in spaces with more than two dimensions. However, as the number of particles exceeds a critical threshold, their movement suddenly shifts to a different, more chaotic state. This abrupt shift is known as a discontinuous phase transition.

The growth of information on the internet has led to an increase in unstructured data, making it difficult to access and utilize. To overcome this challenge, converting unstructured data into structured data through OCR technology is essential. Although OCR is effective at extracting text from images, it also introduces errors that require post-processing to correct. This study combines NLP techniques with traditional OCR to extract information from Indonesian ID cards, utilizing a dataset of 1,000 ID card images. The study's proposed method achieved high extraction accuracy for various fields, with the KPPB field having the lowest F-score of 0.45.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect has been utilized to derive lower bounds for the moments of inertia of three asteroids: 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro. By analyzing light curve data from various sources, period changes resulting from the YORP effect were computed for these asteroids, leading to estimates of the YORP acceleration coefficients. This information enabled the development of spin state evolution models, which in turn facilitated more accurate YORP-derived moment of inertia estimates. The final results are expressed as constraints rather than precise values and are formulated as ratios relative to the bulk density of each asteroid.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure.

Multiple formal models of computation have been developed for continuous functions mapping infinite words to infinite words. M. Sakai established a computable function class, titled SC, that maps infinite words to infinite words. This note focuses on the characteristics of synthesizing Ac automata that map infinite words to their corresponding computable functions. It also explores the conditions under which functions can be realized through composition with other functions, specifically suffix and shift functions.

A machine learning technique is presented to identify multiple coexisting attractors in systems that exhibit complex behavior. Our method leverages the symbolic dynamics of a system to train a neural network, which can generalize and classify the symbolic sequences of new data without being explicitly provided the symbolic sequences of those sequences corresponding to initial conditions not represented in the training data. Through various examples, including a Lorenz system with two basins of attraction and a Chua circuit with four coexisting periodic orbits, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. A particularly notable achievement is our successful classification of a Lorenz system with an extremely weak basin, where we accurately identified and mapped the system's unique and previously unknown basin using our method.

To address scalability issues in nonlinear optimal control, this study proposes a numerical method for calculating the reachable state set within a specified time frame under constraints. The underlying equation, representing the boundary of this set, is a complex variational Hamilton-Jaacs-Isaacs Hamilton equation with the time frame parameter influencing its type. By leveraging the equation's structural properties, the numerical approach efficiently computes the needed subset of the state and time state space. The resulting reachable state set within a defined time frame is then demonstrated for varialia and blow-up equations, both known instances of this broader category.

The functional organization of the ventral temporal cortex has been extensively studied, with evidence pointing to a gradient-like arrangement based on animacy. While some sources suggest animacy is binary, dividing animate and inanimate objects, other evidence indicates it is continuous. To investigate this matter, we used high-resolution fMRI to measure individual-level responses to animate, inanimate natural objects, and Gaussian prime symbols. Using a clustering method, we determined that the anatomy exhibits a binary organization, with the majority of animate objects sharing a similar pattern of brain activation. Furthermore, we found that this clustering pattern is consistent across different species, further supporting the binary nature of the animacy continuum in the ventral temporal cortex.

The study proves the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros or confirms quantum unique ergodicity for GL_2 Hecke-Maass newforms at a calculable pace, supported by the broader conclusion that Dirichlet L-function zeros exert a force pushing zeros of EH_0E L-functions away from the edge and/or diagonal in the general case, absent in the robust zone.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre/postconditions that go beyond safety, encompassing liveness and behavior-similar properties.

The rapid transmission of infectious diseases is significantly influenced by the presence of super-spreading events, which account for a large number of infections through a small number of highly transmissible contacts. To investigate the impact of these events on the pace of an epidemic, we developed a stochastic version of the SIR model that takes into consideration variable transmission probabilities. By comparing our simulation results with analytical predictions and theoretical models from previous research, we found that our approach provides more precise forecasts of the epidemic's progression. We also discovered that the distribution of transmission links follows an exponential pattern, which can be modified by external factors such as intervention measures. Notably, we found that models based on fixed networks and extreme value statistics fail to accurately predict super-spreading events, which has important implications for the planning and response to future epidemics and pandemics.

Let's consider a complex topological vector space, denoted as X, along with the collection L(X) of continuous linear operators that act on X. This paper seeks to expand the concept of codiskcyclicity, initially developed for a solitary operator within L(X), to a broader context of operator sets defined as $\Gamma\subset L(X).$ Some key results regarding codiskcyclic collections of operators are proven, accompanied by a codiskcyclicity criterion. Furthermore, we demonstrate its practical utility by investigating the codiskcyclicity of C_0-semigroups, operator semigroups, and discrete semigroups of operators on X.

The precision of our understanding of how magnetic fields affect complex magnetic phenomena, such as solar flares and coronal mass ejections, relies heavily on accurately measuring vector magnetic fields in the sun's upper atmosphere. A significant challenge in this endeavor is that these atmospheric fields are too weak and short-lived to be directly observed. As a result, researchers have developed various techniques to infer these fields from the patterns they create in the sun's visible light spectrum. Unfortunately, these techniques can introduce systematic errors, or biases, in the inferred measurements, which can vary significantly depending on the specific method used. A study was conducted to investigate the sources and magnitudes of biases in these inferred measurements, with a focus on a widely used technique known as Stokes inversion extended linearly (SISVEL). By examining the bias in inferred magnetic fields across a broad range of conditions, the study utilized both synthetic spectra and real observations from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS). In order to mitigate the introduced biases, correction factors were developed and applied to the data, with a demonstration of their effectiveness using a specific event observed by IRIS. This work paves the way for more accurate and reliable inferred measurements of vector magnetic fields in the sun's upper atmosphere.

A sign problem in Monte Carlo simulations severely hampers the scalability of models with a large number of particles or extended time-series data. In the context of the Hubbard model, this issue can be overcome by utilizing complex-valued artificial neural networks to represent the wave function, enabling efficient solution of the simulated equations at a linear cost in relation to the number of complex numbers. This research also explores the use of complex numbers to provide interpretable parameters for the neural network.

Given a non-erasing free monoid morphism σ and subshifts X and Y, where Y is a factor of X through σ, we explore how the topological entropy h(X) and h(Y) are related. Specifically, we examine whether h(Y) is always less than or equal to h(X) and under what conditions they could be equal. We also investigate if there are scenarios where h(Y) exceeds h(X). A notable discovery by Adamczewski and Bugeaud reveals that for the β-expansion subshift X(2, λ) associated with 2 = ∑(n=0 to ∞) α^n with λ=α, the complexity of X(2, λ) is at most finite, implying that λ must be an algebraic number with a specific property. This leads to the conclusion that if λ is irrational, its topological entropy is at most 1. In addition, if the complexity of X(2, λ) is finite, we can further establish that λ's entropy is strictly less than 1 if the complexity is infinite. These conclusions hold true for a broader class of numbers, including those satisfying a complexity condition through the monoid morphism that maps the base 2 to a polynomial in a free group.

By leveraging previously acquired skills, humans can effortlessly adapt to new tasks with little to no experience.
Our innovative approach, called Retrieval Augmentation for Generalization (RAG2), builds upon existing unsupervised few-shot settings and creates a novel paradigm for unsupervised cross-task generalization.
In RAG2, we establish a connection between the source and target tasks by incorporating general knowledge from the existing few-shot scenario, enabling the model to generate a target task prompt without any task-specific labels.
To achieve this, we employ a two-stage process, where RAG2 first generates pseudo-labels for the target data and then fine-tunes the model using the retrieved information.
Our proposed method shows promising results on unsupervised few-shot text classification and natural language inference tasks, outperforming state-of the-art results.

Optimizing hyperparameters is crucial in deep learning, especially when privacy is protected. Traditional methods like Bayesian optimization, which are used to efficiently tune parameters, do not take into consideration the impact of Bayesian differentially private (BDP) on this process. This study analyzes the effects of BDP on Bayesian optimization, specifically on how it influences the performance of the surrogate model and the perturbation of the acquisition function. A Bayesian optimization method that is private, known as Bayesian optimization under BDP, has been developed to address these issues. This approach selects a set of hyperparameters that is private and ensures efficient convergence of the Bayesian optimization process. Experiments conducted on various real-world datasets for classification and regression demonstrate the superiority of this approach in comparison to other optimization methods that take into consideration the impact of BDP.

For a Coxeter system defined by $W,S$, we define a combinatorial structure known as the invariant bolean complex of the Coxeter group, denoted as $\mathcal{B}(W)$, consisting of the subgroups of $W$ that remain unchanged under conjugation and are themselves isomorphic to $W$. We prove that for a finite Coxeter group, this structure behaves like a boolean lattice. We also explore the properties of these bolean complexes in the context of infinite groups, specifically examining their relationship with the conjugation-isomorphism graph of the group. We further investigate these structures for specific infinite groups, including those with a type $\tilde{C}_n$ presentation, the universal group with two generators and an abelian relation, and the group with an abelian relation between two generators and their inverses.

We developed a comprehensive approach to analyze the chemical composition of 104,000 stars using APOGEE data, spanning a wide range of distances from the galactic center (5 to 15 kpc) and vertical distances from the galactic plane (-4 to +4 kpc). By utilizing a novel two-component model that accounts for stellar metallicity and radial position, along with an advanced distance measurement technique, we created detailed profiles of R20pc and L20pc populations across three distinct regions of the Milky Way disk. These profiles include R20pc and L20pc distributions, as well as their correlations with stellar properties such as rotation, alpha-element to iron abundance ratio, and the abundance of carbon, oxygen, and nitrogen. Furthermore, we examined nitrogen and carbon to oxygen abundance ratios to gain insights into the formation and evolution of the structure of the galactic disk. By comparing our findings to theoretical models and previous studies, we gained a deeper understanding of the chemical history of the Milky Way and the interplay between different elements in the formation and evolution of the galactic disk.

The COVID-19 pandemic in China has led to the rapid dissemination of both genuine news and rumors on the internet. Studying how rumors spread online is crucial to preventing further transmission of the virus. This research focuses on identifying and analyzing the factors behind the rapid propagation of rumors on the internet during the COVID-19 outbreak in China. A logistic regression model was developed to predict the adoption of a rumor over time, and its key drivers were examined. Our findings reveal that media reports significantly influence the spread of rumors in the early stages, while social media usage becomes a more prominent factor in the later stages. Additionally, our study provides a framework for measuring the early spread of rumors that combines web crawling techniques, search engine data analysis, and machine learning methods. This approach can be applied to other public health issues to effectively manage and prevent the outbreak of pandemics.

A comprehensive investigation of planetary nebulae (PNe) within the Fornax cluster has been undertaken, focusing on individual PN objects. This in-depth analysis enables precise distance measurements to the galaxies hosting them with a low level of uncertainty. As a result, absolute magnitude versus luminosity effective temperature diagrams for these galaxies can be created, providing a detailed examination of stellar evolution and PN dynamics within each host galaxy. A high level of resolution is achieved in these studies. This level of detail is not feasible for early-type galaxies in other nearby clusters, such as Coma, due to the high density of PN objects per square arcsecond. Within the three early-type galaxies of the Fornax cluster with a high level of distortion, we have created models to account for the movement and interaction of PN objects, providing accurate distance measurements to each galaxy. These measurements are expressed as ratios to the speed of light, with a level of uncertainty of approximately 2-3%. As a result, velocity distributions of PN objects within these galaxies can be examined, providing a detailed understanding of stellar evolution and PN dynamics within the Fornax cluster. A large database of PN objects has also been created, which can be used for future studies of the Fornax cluster and beyond. This database is available for public use, providing a valuable resource for the astronomical community.

Every day, hospitals around the world handle massive amounts of physiological data from patients, often involving thousands of simultaneous patients and complex computations like pattern recognition and data visualization. These tasks require high-performance processing to be effective. However, existing simulation tools used to evaluate physiological data processing systems are limited in their performance, capping the number of simultaneous patients at a few hundred, which significantly restricts the reliability of the evaluated systems. In response to this challenge, we are proud to introduce LifeStream, a stream processing engine designed for efficient, large-scale physiological data processing. LifeStream excels in this domain by efficiently managing data performance, adaptive caching of program code, and optimized handling of temporary data in memory. Performance tests show that LifeStream can process continuous, real-world physiological datasets with over 10,000 patients, providing significant performance gains compared to existing tools. Specifically, LifeStream offers a 1.9x to 7.1x performance improvement over DuckStream and a 1.3x to 2.5x improvement over Ray.
This research paper proves that timelike Bertrand curves in Euclidean space with positive index must occur in two-dimensional Euclidean subspaces.

The choice of loss function in deep learning models for classification has been widely used, with standard functions such as cross-entropy and sum of squared errors being the norm. Nonetheless, the vast array of loss functions available in the Keras library, numbering in the hundreds, raises the question of whether experimenting with alternative loss functions can yield notable improvements in model performance. To investigate this issue, we developed a novel framework that leverages graph theory to systematically explore and categorize loss functions, resulting in a structured representation of the Keras library. This in turn facilitated a targeted loss function exploration, in contrast to random selection. Our empirical findings demonstrate that, on average, carefully chosen loss functions outperform those randomly picked and even outperform those in prior research, indicating that such experimentation is worth considering in the design of deep learning models for classification tasks.

This research develops a robust numerical framework to analyze the straintype crystallization process within cooling polymer systems. By integrating a thermomechanical model with advanced molecular transformation theories, we simulate the cyclic crystallization and melting of polymers at a microscopic level. A novel numerical technique, combining finite element methods with time-discontinuous Galerkin approaches, enables accurate modeling of displacement fields and temperature variations. Applied to a representative polymer, our results demonstrate the self-sustaining nature of strain-induced crystallization when subjected to cyclic temperature changes. Furthermore, our simulations reveal that temperature decline triggers local crystallization, which in turn accelerates local melting above a critical threshold, ultimately leading to the destruction of the microstructure.

To analyze the impact of external magnetic fields on d-wave superconductivity, we applied a time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau approach to a nematic state, characterized by anisotropic gaps and vortex states with distinct anisotropic properties. Initially, we examined the triplet component of the superconducting gap's Pauli paramagnetism, which exhibits significant anisotropy due to the absence of order parameter deformation and only orbital depairing in the triplet channel. Notably, the diagonal component of the triplet pair symmetry contributes to magnetization, leading to a non-zero average that can be influenced by the pair's orbital orientation. Additionally, we investigated the transverse component's transverse susceptibility, which displays significant anisotropy with its principal axis aligned with the easy axis of the system. In contrast, the scalar component of the gap undergoes only orbital depairing, and its compression along the k-axis results in increased magnetization, with the paramagnetic current displaying significant anisotropy with its principal axis also aligned with the system's easy axis. Finally, we explored the impact of the superconductor's crystalline anisotropy on the system, which influences the degree of paramagnetic anisotropy.

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection methods suffers from reduced resilience to abrupt interference compared to its coherent counterpart. This study analyzes the feasibility of enhancing abrupt differential interference mitigation by examining the underlying mechanisms and limitations of conventional differential detection methods. The analysis reveals that improving performance is possible by modifying the input signal processing, with the optimal performance varying depending on the CPM parameters. Theoretical findings are validated through Monte Carlo simulations for 2-T DPSK under partial response signaling, and experimental results from a CMOS differential detector are also included.

The concept of a quantum field in curved spacetime can be reimagined as a collection of harmonic oscillators, each experiencing the influence of the spacetime's geometry. This perspective allows for the assessment of spacetime's thermodynamic properties, revealing the presence of a quantum phase transition in the Rindler wedge. In the Rindler wedge, the radiation field undergoes a transition from a coherent phase to a squeezed phase as the temperature surpasses a critical threshold. This transition has significant implications for spacetime's quantum properties, particularly in relation to quantum density fluctuations and the quantum error correction capability. These fluctuations and correction capability undergo dramatic changes at the transition point, diverging and vanishing, respectively. These effects are more pronounced in higher-dimensional Rindler wedges and R\'{o}m\'{e}r wedges, where they become infinite and zero at the transition temperature.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an extensive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules that comprise approximately 2.4 million "if-then" relationships.  This atlas of knowledge structures propositions in the form of conditional statements, where each entry consists of an activity or object in an "then" statement and a corresponding "if" statement providing additional information.  To our benefit, this vast amount of implicit reasoning capabilities can be leveraged to pursue AI systems grounded in commonsense. We utilized the open-source Prodigy annotation tool to efficiently collect high-quality annotations through crowd-sourcing.  Our benchmark demonstrates that utilizing ATOMIC as a knowledge base enables powerful artificial intelligence to perform insightful, logical inference.

Portfolio management is a critical aspect of finance that requires making sound decisions to make optimal investment decisions. Due to the intricate and dynamic nature of financial markets, making these decisions is an arduous task. In this paper, we develop a hybrid-quantum implementation of the Harrod-Ohlson algorithm to facilitate portfolio optimization. We adapt the algorithm to accommodate the constraints of Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices, and demonstrate its functionality using the Qiskit framework on actual NISQ hardware. Furthermore, we explore alternative optimization methods and evaluate their efficacy. Our research reveals that the Harrod-Ohlson algorithm can successfully optimize investment portfolios within the constraints of NISQ devices.

To enhance the accuracy of speech recognition systems, this study focuses on leveraging auxiliary information from text data. A bidirectional attention mechanism is employed to selectively utilize relevant text information, while filtering out irrelevant noise. A simple yet effective data augmentation technique is proposed to create training samples by aligning transcriptions of audio with corresponding text. This approach enables a speech recognition model to undergo multi-modal training, integrating audio and text data. Experimental results on the Librispeech dataset demonstrate the model's capability to learn effectively from multi-modal data and achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art speech recognition models. Furthermore, using pre-trained multi-modal models for inference allows for speech recognition systems to perform robustly even in scenarios with limited audio data.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a random parking model, specifically the uniform model, where multiple drivers with distinct preferences choose parking spots based on predetermined routes. A set of parking functions and an associated probability distribution that mimics the model's behavior in the long run are defined. In a model involving $n$ drivers and roads with varying capacities, we analyze the first parking locations and determine their asymptotic distribution under different road capacity conditions. Specifically, when the road capacities are equal, the first parking locations converge to a non-random value, whereas, when the road capacities grow at different rates, the first parking locations follow power law distributions with different exponents.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires with normal metallic contacts at both ends reveal intricate granular behavior in their non-equilibrium states. Researchers observed significant variations in the quantum phase-slips occurring within the nanowires, attributed to differences in their intrinsic disorder. A study was conducted on NbNNanowires, exhibiting a wide range of phase-slip behaviors, from highly localized to completely gapless. The influence of in-sample variations on the coherent quantum phase-slip-Andreev bound state dynamics were found to be a key factor in the observed granularities.

Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that typically deals with limited view changes using optimization techniques, our method aims to surpass viewpoint limitations by leveraging a dual graph representation to model video sequences. This representation captures both temporal and spatial dependencies, enabling robust interpolation and interpolation for missing data. To extract discriminative features from raw video, we employ a Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network, utilizing a Generative Adversarial Network framework to ensure the temporal coherence and realism of synthesized frames. Experiments demonstrate the superiority of our method in novel view video prediction, outperforming state-of-the-art interpolation methods and achieving satisfactory results with a minimal training dataset.

In an interference pattern created by two atomic states with different momenta, we identified signs of atoms transitioning between s and p orbitals, which normally do not interact, as a result of tunneling through an optical lattice. This phenomenon, first predicted in 1980, is being visually demonstrated for the first time with a clear and straightforward setup, providing a straightforward way to study transitions between different orbital types.

The Ω-baryon, first predicted by Gell-Mann and Ne'eman in 1964, has a theoretical mass of 1690 MeV/c², with a predicted total width of 8-16 MeV/c². However, due to its narrow resonance and low production probability, experimental data on this particle remains limited. Using the J/ψ decay, we conducted an analysis of J/ψ → K^-K^-K^+K^+ to identify and examine the J/ψ decay channel of the Ω-baryon, specifically the J/ψ → K^-K^-Ω^+ process. Through this examination, we discovered 124 events of J/ψ → K^-K^-Ω^+ process and conducted a detailed study of J/ψ decay involving the -/- mode of the Ω-baryon.

Airresuspension of infectious aerosols due to human activities indoors can significantly contribute to the transmission of respiratory infections. Mathematical models that simulate the mixing of indoor air have been valuable tools for investigating this issue. These models typically assume that air contaminants, including infectious agents, are uniformly distributed throughout the space, a assumption that may not hold true in rooms with varying degrees of air movement and turbulence. This paper examines the suitability of uniform mixing models in predicting the transmission of respiratory infections in a specific indoor setting: an urban bus. A previous study by the same author used a well-mixed model to successfully predict SARS-CoV-2 transmission on a bus, but there was a risk of overfitting the data. To address this, this paper explores ways to fit well-mixed models to available data, discusses the limitations and potential sources of model error, and investigates how model fitting can be improved. It is hoped that these insights will guide future studies and encourage the use of detailed indoor mixing models in epidemiological studies of respiratory infections transmitted indoors.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect (SP) in ferromagnetic Cobalt layers adjacent to heavy element interfaces is investigated, with a focus on its dependence on the Co layer thickness in [N Cobalt/(M Heavy)/O Oxide] superlattices. Experimental data reveals that the SP parameter λ varies with the number of Cobalt layers N, and its behavior is significantly influenced by interface scattering. In contrast to conventional expectations, the mean free path of the SP parameter increases with N when interface scattering is taken into account. This is corroborated by calculations using the Kubo formula and the Non-Equilibrium Green's Function method, which show that the SP parameter's behavior is determined by the interplay between bulk and interface contributions. Notably, the interface contribution exhibits periodic oscillations, leading to a non-monotonic dependence of λ on N. This study emphasizes the critical role of interface scattering in determining the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect in [N Cobalt/(M Heavy)/O Oxide] superlattices.

This study derives the exact fractional dimensional Schrödinger equation in a generalised Mie-type potential framework, using Jumarie type fractional derivative. A fractional dimensional effective potential is obtained through a transformation of the force, and an analytic solution is found using the fractional series expansion method. Key parameters for the fractional dimensional effect are identified, and the fractional dimensional ground state energy is plotted.

We analyze how neural networks acquire their inherent Lipschitz continuity, which is a property that is rarely discussed. We then connect this to a more commonly studied concept, convexity, specifically in the context of a neural network's activation function, which is known to be convex. This relationship is particularly evident when dealing with classification tasks. Next, we explore two methods for making neural networks more Lipschitz continuous, which is an important feature for practical applications. We find that both methods, one involving a reparametrization of the network's weights and the other by training the network with an additional loss function, successfully reduce the inherent convexity of the network, which is a desirable outcome. Numerical experiments support these findings.

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan dilepton production and calculate precise predictions for it using third-generation gauge vector leptoquark models. By applying the fixed-order expansion of the Einstein-Cartan theory to General Relativity, we derive these predictions for muon and tau pair production at the LHC, obtaining values for the new contact interaction scale $\Lambda$ that are consistent with observed data. Specifically, we find that for $\tau^+\tau^-$ production, values of $\Lambda$ in the TeV range are within reach of current and future LHC experiments. To facilitate this, we provide updated predictions for various LHC processes, including $\mu^+\mu^-$, $e^+e^-$, $e^+\tau^+$, $e^-\tau^-$, $\mu^+\tau^-$, $\mu^-\tau^+$, $\mu^+\tau^+\tau^-$, $\mu^-\tau^-\tau^+$, $\tau^+\tau^+\tau^-$, and $\tau^-\tau^-\tau^+$ pair production, as well as $t$-quark associated production with these pairs.

Medical imaging techniques like CT and PET often expose patients to high levels of ionizing radiation, posing health risks. To mitigate this, PET images can be generated using alternative modalities like ultrasound or MRI through machine learning models. However, existing methods struggle when low-dose PET images are desired due to the fact that learning datasets consist of high-dose images. In response to this limitation, a novel approach has been developed that enables direct generation of low-dose PET images from ultrasound images and patient information. This approach utilizes a neural network to simultaneously learn simultaneous transformations of MRI data and ultrasound images for better performance. To ensure robustness against OOD data, uncertainty estimation has been incorporated into the model, allowing it to quantify its confidence in predictions and reject predictions with high uncertainty. The proposed method has been evaluated on multiple datasets and shows improved reconstruction quality and uncertainty-awareness compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

A linguistic concept known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations is achieved by linking new information to previous discourse. This study explores the connection between CT and advanced artificial intelligence systems called neural coreference resolution (CRR) models. We developed a neural CRR framework based on the principles of CT, resulting in a system that excels at resolving complex references in lengthy textual inputs. By incorporating the structural information of discourse from the early stages of neural CRR architecture, our system effectively manages inputs with varying levels of complexity and extensive discourse lengths. Experimental results show that our system outperforms the state-of-the-art neural CRR methods in the Microsost corpus and manages to resolve previously unsolved high and double definite pronoun types.

Accurate distance estimation between WiFi devices is essential for a wide range of applications, including indoor navigation, mobile marketing, and mobile payments. This paper investigates the various machine learning approaches that can be employed to determine the distance between devices based on WiFi signal strength. It outlines the fundamental concepts of supervised learning, outlines the steps for creating a dataset, and outlines the different machine learning algorithms that can be utilized to solve this problem.

The beam breakup instability poses a significant challenge for particle accelerators, and as energy recovery linacs strive for higher luminosity, it is crucial to manage this issue effectively. A recent study delves into filling pattern influences on beam breakup instability in future high-energy recovery linacs, taking into account coupled bunch effects. Analytical findings demonstrate that patterns with higher bunch numbers at both low and high energy levels contribute to improved stability, and coupled bunch effects further enhance this benefit. By leveraging the broad dynamic range of energy recovery linacs, carefully designed future filling patterns can significantly improve stability and enable higher beam currents and luminosity.

This research focuses on highly stretched, non-entangled polymer brushes of various shapes, including spheres, surfaces, and interfaces, and derives new exclusion zone theories for these configurations. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint every other vertex in the graph. This capability is measured by the minimum size of R known as the metric dimension of G. We are exploring a variation of this idea where a point's location is only partially identifiable beyond the graph's boundary. This incomplete identifiability is measured by points that are fully distinguishable from one another based on their shortest path differences, denoted by α and the minimum such value, denoted by τ(G). This metric dimension concept is significant in various fields including robotics, network systems, and bioinformatics. However, its application in confined environments requires a modified approach, leading to the development of the truncated metric dimension with two corresponding parameters, τ*(G) and β, under specific conditions. This new parameter also has an integer range defined similar to the traditional metric dimension. We are currently investigating the properties of this new parameter and its relationship with other graph characteristics.

Researchers have developed a novel application for machine learning, specifically a learning algorithm, to interpret large-scale astronomical data from the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. This algorithm is used to create an advanced visualization tool, the SHINE, which generates a 3D representation of the universe's electromagnetic spectrum. This depiction is based on comprehensive data collected over three years from the Fermi-LAT instrument, encompassing over 99 percent of the sky's gamma-ray emissions. Notably, various source classifications, including cosmic background radiation, radio galaxies, and gamma-ray bursts, have been incorporated into this visualization. By applying an individual time-frame analysis and geographic classification method, this tool has resulted in a visualization that highlights areas with higher variability.

A social welfare maximization algorithm is examined in the context of a fixed set of agent utility functions. It is given access to aFD (fully dictatorial) protocol, in which one agent picks an allocation from the feasible set of possible allocations. The algorithm's performance is measured in comparison to social welfare, taking into consideration the total welfare of all agents in a given allocation. We establish theoretical constraints on this algorithm's effectiveness, considering various constraints on utility functions and types of restrictions on dictatorial protocols. In contrast to other protocols such as randomized dictatorship or sequential dictatorship, we demonstrate that social welfare can be significantly optimized by a algorithm in the presence of concave utilities through a dictatorship protocol.

Resolving main-belt asteroids into individual components is challenging due to their brief scintillation events. This difficulty is compounded for solitary asteroids with extremely low albedo variations or those comprising indistinguishable small fragments. This scintillation analysis, however, is effective at detecting binary systems, particularly in wide-field surveys like Pan-STARRS1, by distinguishing scintillation from variability. This analysis leverages over a million known main-belt asteroids from the database, searching for short-period short-semission binary asteroids. This search identifies 140 asteroids that are binary candidates, with over a thousand additional known asteroids awaiting confirmation. These time-scale characteristics, when input into the Rice model, forecast mutual event frequencies that can be verified through long-term monitoring. This search also establishes selection criteria for time-scale characteristic features in binary asteroids, facilitating their identification in wide-field survey data.

This research supplements the findings related to the specified context, model, and estimation methods initially presented by Liang (2021). The paper presents some related statistical conclusions and estimates connected to the network in relation to the PL model. It also explores a specific PL estimation method known as GMM based on a particular set of residuals and remains available for use by other scholars. A particular GMM method for assessing NP effects is also examined and demonstrated in the appendix of this work.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for both the integral and differential operators. Specifically, four distinct product rule formulas are obtained, two quotient rule formulas are derived, and four distinct chain rule formulas are derived.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by a specific goal, in this case leading a player to a target, and demonstrating the value of a theory-of-mind approach to achieve this.

The complex folding dynamics of knotted proteins are influenced by various factors, including genetic, topological, and environmental elements. While the general principles governing knotted protein folding are understood, the specific mechanisms remain elusive. By incorporating the concept of effective chain length, we developed a framework to analyze the topological characteristics of figure-eight knotted proteins in their natural state, which revealed correlations between chain dimensions and local structure complexity. Furthermore, we utilized stochastic models to simulate potential folding pathways from the native configurations, determining that figure-eight knots can result from either the induction or trapping mechanisms, with each model displaying distinct characteristics. These insights provide a basis for investigating protein figure-eight knot topology, analyzing evolutionary relationships, and exploring protein folding dynamics.

Given a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism $\phi$ of $\mathbb{T}^4$, we investigate the syametric mapping stiffness property within the subgroup of diffeomorphisms $\delta \in \mathrm{Ham}(\mathbb{T}^4,\omega)$ that are conjugate to $\phi$ through a symplectic isomorphism of the pair $(\mathbb{T}^4,\omega)$. We establish that this property is inconjugate stable within the symplectic mapping class group of $\mathbb{T}^4$ with respect to the Kaehler form's blowup $\omega_{Bl_1 \mathbb{T}^4}$.
