A detailed examination of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone theorem is undertaken, contrasting its implications in both quantum field theories and those exhibiting $\pm i$ anomalies. This investigation draws heavily upon an in-depth analysis of pions within the framework of Quantum Chromodynamics. A central aspect of this research involves formulating the anomalous theorem in a general manner using the Ward-Takahashi identities of quantum field theory. A key component of this research is the development of a local, gauge-invariant, and renormalizable effective Lagrangian for the Nambu-Goldstone bosons of the chiral anomaly. This enables an explicit calculation of the axial anomaly's impact on the axial-axial scattering process in Quantum Chromodynamics. A significant byproduct of this research is the derivation of the axial-axial anomaly's contribution to the axial-axial-axial interaction vertex, filling a notable gap in existing knowledge.

Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can significantly enhance models' ability to generalize. Although effective, this approach is often impractical for tasks like natural language generation due to the high cost of training. A promising solution lies in pretraining language models on phrasal counterfactuals generated by large models, as suggested by our research. We further investigate replacing the common "on the other hand" phrase with the corresponding counterfactual phrase to enhance training efficiency. Our pretraining method, named DISCO, is further developed into a counterfactual knowledge distillation stage, utilizing structure and style from a teacher model to create sentences with paired actual and counterfactual statements. Experiments show that DISCO leads to a 5% improvement in generalization for entity resolution and up to 10% for tasks using phrasal counterfactuals.

Research into remote epitaxy has been hindered by limitations in equipment, surface preparation, and the need for vacuum conditions. Graphene has been proposed as an alternative substrate that enables remote epitaxy without the need for high vacuum, although conflicting results have been obtained when growing complex materials on it. This study focuses on the unique interface between Cu2OAlS2 and graphene/gallium arsenide, taking advantage of van der Waals epitaxy to explore interface engineering. By deliberately introducing interface defects, we were able to grow a high-quality Cu2OAlS2 film on a specific area of the graphene, achieving high carrier mobility of 10,000 cm2/Vs. This demonstrates the ability to control interface interactions and paves the way for growing sophisticated materials on two-dimensional materials.

A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of encoding process called the Gray image of a code that has properties derived from $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive code, specifically when a prime number $p$ is taken into account. In an attempt to examine the rank and dimension characteristics of the images of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}}$-additive codes, researchers have studied the Ranks and Dimension of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}}$-linear codes. In the course of this investigation, they have established specific properties of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}}$-linear codes, including an intricate relationship between the rank of a code and its kernel, as well as a method for constructing high-rank $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}}$-linear codes.

Conditional GANs have shown great potential in generating data with specific labels, but when it comes to labels that can coexist, current Conditional GAN approaches fall short. A new evaluation method, Multi-Label Classification Benchmark, along with a proposed framework, Multi-label Sample Miners (MSM), are presented to overcome these limitations. The key concept behind MSM is leveraging an untrained variational autoencoder to generate high-quality samples from limited labeled data, which are then used to train a Conditional GAN classifier. Experimental results show that when applied to real-world datasets, the proposed framework can effectively create samples with multiple, accurate labels.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra from a given state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction can be viewed as a kind of inverse procedure, integrating a natural transformation into a natural isomorphism. This insight can be categorically expressed as an adjoint relationship between functors operating within the 2-category of strict 2-functors from a free one-object 2-category.

The origin of high-energy gamma-rays in nearby galaxies is still unknown.
Whether these gamma-rays are produced by jets or disks in active galactic nuclei
is still debated.
We investigate the possibility of gamma-rays being produced by magnetically
arrested disks, a model that can account for gamma-ray production in both the
disk and the jet regions.
Using the Fermi-LAT gamma-ray data, we identify the likely sources
of gamma-rays and their corresponding jet/ disk classifications.
We focus on four nearby AGN with extensive gamma-ray signals and compact
cores, where the jets or disks are believed to be dominated by the magnetic
fields.
Our analysis shows that magnetically controlled disks can produce gamma-rays
through two primary mechanisms.
First, magnetic reconnection in the ADAF can occur, leading to gamma-rays
being produced near the core.
Second, gamma-rays can be produced by jets launched from
knots in the magnetosphere of an accretion disk.
Our analysis also highlights that jet/ disk models can be further complicated
by the presence of a blazar or a galaxy-scale disk.
Focusing on the main gamma-ray production mechanism, we develop a MARDK model
that combines jet/ disk dynamics with magnetic recombination, resulting in
gamma-rays being produced in both regions.
This model can be tested by analyzing the spatial distribution of
gamma-rays and the spectral characteristics of various emission lines.

Cardiac diseases significantly contribute to global mortality, and early detection is crucial for effective treatment. Traditional diagnostic methods involve auscultation, where a stethoscope is used to listen to heart sounds, and any abnormal tones are identified by a medical professional. To enhance accuracy and consistency in cardiac condition diagnosis, automatic classification systems based on auscultatory data have been developed. This research focuses on creating a robust cardiac sound classification model capable of accurately diagnosing conditions from noisy and altered recordings. Experiments were conducted on the noisy Inria dataset and an ultrasound simulation dataset to evaluate the performance. A deep noise cancellation technique was applied to recorded sounds contaminated with ambient noise, and an ultrasound simulation model was utilized to replicate the sound distortion experienced during clinical auscultation with a stethoscope. Furthermore, the effects of different levels of noise and distortion on cardiac sound classification were systematically examined. Results show that after noise removal and applying a simulated distortion level of 20dB, cardiac sound classification performance declined by 14.3%, 10.1%, 10.4%, 10.5%, and 10.1% for arrhythmia, systolic hypertension, diastolic hypertension, combined hypertension, and cardiac hypertrophy classes, respectively.

The proliferation of wearable devices has significantly transformed personal healthcare monitoring. Nevertheless, effectively training high-quality medical diagnosis models for such devices poses a substantial challenge. Traditional methods that rely on large datasets are difficult to implement due to privacy concerns and the high costs associated with data collection. In wearable settings, where models must operate on limited devices with constrained memory and processing power, even successfully trained models may not function effectively. To overcome these obstacles, we introduce a novel federated transfer learning method called FedHealth. FedHealth employs a wearable device as an initial model and uses federated training to adapt the model across multiple centers with different amounts of data. We evaluate FedHealth for two common medical conditions, hypertension and sleep apnea, and compare its performance to that of a conventional model trained through centralized training. Experimental results indicate that FedHealth can accurately diagnose medical conditions and outperform the conventional model. Notably, FedHealth demonstrates its versatility and efficiency by effectively adapting to new conditions with minimal data through the application of transfer learning in a federated setting.
This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid hedge fund practitioners in navigating complex strategies.

In large-scale organizations, recruiting involves interviewing numerous candidates for available positions. To effectively manage this process, recruiters require support in coordinating interviews, scheduling, and logistics. This paper introduces an innovative approach to automate parts of this process by applying machine learning techniques. Our method leverages application data to automatically extract features and build a model that predicts successful candidates. We evaluated our approach using real application data from a prominent technology company, comparing it to a basic selection method. The results show that our machine learning-based approach outperforms the baseline, indicating its potential to enhance recruitment processes in big organizations.

This study tackles a complex control issue involving unpredictable cost fluctuations at specific moments, aiming to minimize the time until a target is reached. The problem's parameters, including the cost volatility, fluctuate over time in a way that can change in both directions. Our analysis of the associated optimal strategy reveals that there is a specific point beyond which it becomes advantageous to fulfill the objective despite the associated cost. Our validated numerical approach enables us to investigate the variability of this strategy in response to changes in the cost volatility.

To explore the significance of asymmetric leptoquark pairs at the Large Hadron Collider, our study focuses on scalar leptoquarks from the first generation and their possible types, specifically $S_1$ and $S_2$. As asymmetric parameters increase, leptoquark production in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, with a cross-section of 1 nanobarns, becomes feasible. Our analyses of decay modes, including $\mu e$ and $\mu \mu$ final states, reveal that leptoquark pair events predominantly consist of same-sign combinations. We identify strategies to enhance detection efficiency and propose using leptoquark production to create high-momentum muons, which can then serve as probes for strange quark distribution at high momentum fractions. Furthermore, we demonstrate how asymmetric parameters can enhance the sensitivity of leptoquark searches and explore the potential for single leptoquark production to set constraints on their mass.

We've used a new subthermal excitation model for interstellar clouds to reanalyze the non-LTE behavior of specific interstellar lines, namely the far-infrared C I lines. This model-based approach allows us to obtain more precise estimates of CO abundance ratios relative to molecular gas in galaxies. Replacing the traditional CO fraction fCO, we've defined a new ratio R, which we believe is a more reliable indicator that can be applied to a broader range of galaxies. By examining 100 galaxies with extensive spectral data, we found that the subthermal nature of these clouds results in a consistent overestimation of R, which we believe is a universal effect. We found that the R ratio is overestimated by a factor of ~2.5 on average, which we believe is significant and may have implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution. We've also proposed a new version of the R2020 density estimator that we believe is more reliable than existing methods.

Hamming distance effectively measures how dissimilar two sequences are, making it a useful tool in various applications like gene sequence analysis and detecting transmitted errors in data networks. A significant issue that arises is determining the most probable original sequence from multiple similar sequences, known as the sequence reconstruction problem. In this study, an algorithm is developed to solve this problem for permutations under a specific distance metric, called Hamming distance, within a defined time limit of O(n^3) operations. Furthermore, the precision of a constructed sequence is guaranteed to improve with a higher confidence level, as demonstrated by specific mathematical inequalities in the research.

Researchers anticipate that pulsar timing arrays will soon detect gravitational wave backgrounds, potentially pinpointing their origin. If not caused by supermassive black hole mergers, identifying pulsar-generating signals demands high-precision waveforms, which currently don't exist for highly elliptical binary systems. This work delivers 3.5 post-Newtonian-accurate timing-resonant waveforms, a necessary precursor to this existing gap, and demonstrates a compressed computing basis that accelerates fitting speed by a factor of ten when modeling past PTA data with $\chi^2$ minimization.

profile and two semi-infinite tails extending in opposite directions, a speed
process converges in the hydrodynamic limit to its Ornamented Universal limit.

This study examines various mathematical models developed to analyze the ongoing pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2. As we move into the mid-phase of the epidemic, we've gathered and compared different models that model its progression. A significant number of these models include detailed assessments of how factors such as population movement, case isolation, travel restrictions, and non-pharmaceutical interventions have influenced the epidemic's course. A key aspect of this analysis involves exploring the limitations and potential of these models, particularly in light of available empirical data.

We theoretically investigate coherent conversion between spinor atoms and diatomic molecules through photon-absorbing molecules made of three identical bosonic atoms. By applying an external magnetic field and a specific laser frequency, we show that conversion can be significantly enhanced, leading to either complete conversion or equilibrium between atoms and molecules under a high recombination rate. Our model takes into account strong interatomic interactions and allows for various molecular states, and our findings are supported by numerical simulations.

Our proposed DNA storage scheme, SCARE, addresses two key challenges in real-life applications: representing hierarchical data and managing data updates. In response to the challenge of hierarchy, SCARE leverages a hash function to generate a unique identifier for each data fragment, resulting in a distinctive combination of fragments that efficiently encodes the given hierarchy. In addressing data updates, SCARE overcomes a major limitation of existing codes by utilizing a two-layered hash function to create redundant fragments, thereby enabling efficient deletion and modification of data. SCARE code achieves a high coding rate of 0.65, outperforming comparable codes, and theoretical analysis of its performance is also presented. A comparative analysis with state-of-the-art codes demonstrates SCARE code's superiority in addressing both hierarchical data and data updates in DNA storage.

Precise and efficient hydrological forecasting is crucial for minimizing damage caused by natural disasters. However, accurately modeling river flow requires significant computational resources due to the complex numerical models used. Researchers have recently explored the potential of deep learning to simplify hydrological modeling, but these models also struggle to efficiently handle changes in river topography. In this study, we present a lightweight machine learning approach using a neural network to predict water surface elevation from river geometry and water level inputs. By training on a synthetic 2D river dataset, we achieved highly accurate results with minimal computational cost. Moreover, we found that these models can be easily transferred to different hydrological environments and provide robust predictions even when the river geometry is not directly measurable.

HDR photography aims to broaden the range of brightness depicted in an image. Historically, this required manually taking multiple images at different exposure levels and blending them together. Contemporary smartphone cameras can also produce HDR effects automatically. In this work, we investigate the methods employed by leading commercial mobile devices to achieve this, focusing on five top-rated brands. We assess the performance of these systems by deliberately varying camera settings for static and moving subjects, and compare the results with single-exposure photographs. Our findings offer guidance for developers seeking to enhance their high-dynamic-range algorithms.

Causal deep learning is an emerging and significant area within the broader field of artificial intelligence. It aims to create robust and versatile representations of data using patterns and structures found in causal graphs through various neural network methods. This work explores the use of neural networks to exploit certain features, such as independence, factorization, and conditional independence, within a dataset. It categorizes existing research into three main sections, covering studies on (i) certain representations, such as entropy, (ii) the absence of relationships between variables, and (iii) conditional independence, and discusses potential future directions for investigation. We also highlight key resources, including datasets, benchmarks, and tools, that are valuable for researchers in this field.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work.

This research involves comparing multiple multilevel preconditioners for solving complex cardiac mechanics simulations using finite elements. To make the preconditioners more efficient and scalable for large-scale computations, a particular type of multigrid algorithm known as geometric preconditioner was utilized. To ensure efficient parallel processing, two distinct multilevel data structures were compared: traditional block tridiagonal multilevel (BTML) and a more innovative communication-avoiding multilevel (CAMML) approach. The latter was further divided into two variants, CAMML with diagonal blocking (CAMMLDB) and a linear version (CAMMLL). The study employed a sophisticated three-dimensional heart model and tested various multilevel preconditioners using different grid refinements. The results revealed that the CAMML family of multigrid solvers, particularly the diagonal blocking variant, offered improved scalability and robustness in solving complex simulations. The research also explored the effects of different time integration methods and the impact of varying mesh refinement strategies on multigrid solver performance. The study provides valuable insights for future developments in multilevel solvers for complex simulations.

Standard diffusion models fail to accurately describe the movement of many particles, particularly in complex environments. This issue is compounded when the distribution of particles deviates from a Gaussian pattern. Research has shown that a key factor contributing to this behavior is the fluctuation of local diffusivity, with its timescale and intensity significantly influencing this process. Research methods involved simulating a large number of stochastic paths using a modified Langevin equation, and subsequent analysis of these paths revealed their relationship to direct diffusivity statistics through scaling laws. These findings were validated through simulations of a large ensemble of experimental data from colloidal particles moving within an ensemble of liquid droplets.

A fundamental theory of optical resonator and waveguide modes is presented, which
accounts for linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions. The approach utilizes Green's
theorem, Maxwell's equations, and a fundamental theorem of linear algebra to
derive conservation of linear and nonlinear energy within a confined space.
This enables the determination of all optical field parameters from a finite set of
meaningful physical quantities. The generalized framework is applicable to a wide
range of photonic structures, including optical waveguides, microresonators, and
microdisk devices. The theory is illustrated with examples from rectangular
waveguides to complex spiral photonic crystals.

A recent study proposes a novel deep learning method to reconstruct highly incomplete turbulent flow data with exceptional precision. By integrating generative adversarial networks, this model achieves sub-pixel accuracy in its reconstructions and effectively mimics the statistical characteristics of turbulent flow. In contrast to previous deep learning techniques, this approach requires no explicit training on regression tasks. Instead, it leverages an adversarial training process to enhance the realism of generated images. In highly complex, nonlinear scenarios typical of turbulent flow, this model demonstrates superior performance, outperforming existing deep learning approaches in reconstructing flow images from partial measurements across a wide range of Reynolds numbers.

Recently, reinforcement learning breakthroughs have primarily been confined to fixed tasks, whereas reinforcement learning systems that embrace its potential to leverage experience across changing tasks and time have lagged behind. This shortfall has spurred the development of lifelong reinforcement learning approaches, but there is little in the public domain to facilitate and assess future experiments in this field. This paper introduces Lifelong Reinforcement Learning Assessment Environment (L2Explorer), a novel assessment platform designed to provide a comprehensive set of environments for lifelong reinforcement learning studies. L2Explorer encompasses a diverse array of platforms, encompassing both continuous and discrete action spaces, gradual and sudden task transitions, and varying degrees of task relationship. It also includes a set of gradual parameter adjustment policies to facilitate controlled experimentation. As an open-source assessment environment, L2Explorer is a multifaceted tool that can be utilized for designing and testing lifelong reinforcement learning algorithms, as well as other applications that involve a series of related tasks.

Understanding business processes is crucial for improving organizational performance and achieving process-related goals. Process mining has emerged as a powerful tool for process analysis, offering an alternative to traditional approaches. However, process data is often complex and requires specialized knowledge to interpret, posing a challenge for non-experts. This research focuses on developing innovative monitoring and discovery methods for declarative processes that leverage first-order logic and process traces. To make these methods more accessible, we present accessible visualizations of process anomalies and workflow patterns based on process logs. Our approach generates automated monitoring algorithms and flow anomaly detection methods that produce user-friendly reports and visualizations. We have integrated our methods into a prototype system and evaluated it with a case study involving real-world data. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in producing high-quality visualizations and analysis results that are easily understandable for non-experts.

This note provides an overview and some fresh findings in the area of interest to geometers, physicists, and algebraists concerned with the study of moduli spaces. We review the fundamental concepts of geometric and tropical compactifications, then delve into more complex subjects including geometric and tropical blow-ups, as well as their interconnections.

By incorporating a bulge-to-total mass ratio (BTR) fit into the SCALES dataset using UV-to-IR mass estimation, we examined how star formation in galaxies correlates with the BTR ratio, particularly in massive galaxies. Our investigation reveals a strong correlation between the BTR ratio and the specific star formation rate (sSFR) for galaxies with masses exceeding $10^{10.3}M_{\sun}$, indicating that bulge growth is the primary factor driving the characteristic "turnover" in the mass-sFR relationship at higher masses. For these massive galaxies, we found that the BTR ratio and far-ultraviolet (FUV) light distribution are closely linked, with high sSFR galaxies exhibiting low BTR ratios and concentrated, high sSFR galaxies displaying high BTR ratios. We further observed that in massive galaxies, bulge growth is more closely associated with the total mass than the specific star formation rate (sSFR). Moreover, we found that the relationship between the BTR ratio and stellar mass is consistent across low and high mass galaxies, whereas the connection between sSFR and stellar mass varies significantly, demonstrating that the "knee" in the mass-sFR relation is universal and not species-dependent. This paper presents a novel approach to conducting sentiment analysis in one language using data from two distinct sentiment sources in another language. Through experiments, our method successfully identifies both under one unified class in the target language. Our approach involves training a neural network to recognize patterns indicative of sentiment in the source language, enabling accurate classification in the target language. The network utilizes back-translations of target sentences into the source language and compares them to source sentences, allowing for accurate sentiment classification in the target language. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance compared to existing techniques in multiple domains, including product and news texts in English.

X-ray imaging is widely used in medical diagnosis due to its efficiency and non-invasive nature. However, interpreting X-ray images calls for skilled professionals, as they can be time-consuming and subjective. To address this challenge, this study develops a method to identify patients at high risk of ICU admission among those infected with COVID-19, based on X-ray images. The proposed approach involves using a deep learning technique that automatically extracts image features and integrates them with clinical data, such as oxygen saturation and age. This combined data is then used to train an ensemble classifier to predict the likelihood of ICU admission. The proposed method is evaluated on a dataset of 1,058 X-ray images from COVID-19 patients, and the results show that it can accurately predict ICU admission with an area under the curve value of 0.91. This high level of accuracy highlights the potential of our approach to assist in identifying patients at risk of severe disease progression, thus helping to prioritize medical resources.

The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory.

Visual relationship detection (VRD) aims to identify relationships between objects within an image. Existing false positive analysis methods in object detection do not adequately address the issue of false positives in VRN. We introduce a novel dataset, VSD, comprising 100,000 images with single-object relationships and 100,000 plausible false positive relationships. We conduct a new category-agnostic VRD task, where the model is not aware of the false positive nature of certain relationships. We examine the model's performance using metrics such as the F-score and average relation length. Our analysis reveals the model's tendency to generate short and high-frequency relations, especially in the context of false positives. We also explore the influence of scene context on the model's behavior. VSD serves as a new tool for analyzing and mitigating false positives in complex multi-object scenarios.

We've conducted an in-depth analysis of a galaxy group at a distance of 440 megaparsecs, focusing on a star-forming galaxy group at a young cosmic epoch. The main galaxy, designated as z82, has moved from a large, inactive galaxy with low formation rates to a compact, inactive galaxy with no visible formation rates. We've built a high-resolution, 3D model of its star distribution and movement based on existing data. This model reveals a massive, inactive bulge with a mass of approximately 10 to the 10.5 solar masses, encased in a non-spherical, inactive disk that has little to no active star formation. Beyond this, there's a distant, compact, inactive galaxy with a formation rate of approximately 10 to the 10 solar masses per year. Comparing this model to available data reveals a connection between the inactive galaxy and a quiescent, irregular galaxy type. Simulations reveal a connection between the interaction between the two galaxies and the formation of the inactive bulge and the cessation of active star formation. These findings suggest that interactions between galaxies can lead to the formation of inactive bulges and the cessation of active star formation in galaxy groups at a young cosmic epoch.

Recently, a thorough analysis of solar observations from November 7, 2004 was conducted using data from multiple satellites, including ACE, WIND, SOHO, and NOAA-19. These records revealed the discovery of a significant event in which neutrons from the sun broke down rapidly, followed by a powerful type II solar radio burst and an intense stream of protons. The initial rate of this proton stream was moderate at 2.4 x 10^8 particles per square centimeter per second per steradian, but it quickly escalated to a highly directional event with a initial rate of 6.1 x 10^9 particles per square centimeter per second. The source of this proton storm was linked to a complex solar eruption consisting of two distinct types of explosions that occurred in separate regions of the sun, with one being a highly destructive combination of solar flares and an associated solar eruption, and the other a strong solar flares and an associated solar eruption. Magnetic field models suggested that the first explosion's ejecta reached the site of the second explosion, leading to the observed rate of the proton stream. The characteristics of this event matched the expected behavior of particles from two distinct types of solar flares, with the first explosion's field model leading to the observed rate of the proton stream.

A rapidly rotating F-type star, known as HADS 1, with a period of 4 days and 1 hour, presents a puzzle since stars of its mass should be spinning much slower. This unusual behavior is especially striking given that HADS 1 is located in the young Pismis-1 stellar cluster, where stars are estimated to be between 1.4 and 3.4 million years old. To understand the angular momentum dynamics of young, massive stars, we studied HADS 1 using the Gaia DR3 parallax and radial velocity data, along with high-resolution spectroscopy to measure the system's properties. Our analysis suggests that GJ 113, a possible binary companion to HADS 1 at a distance of 1.4 arcseconds, could be physically linked and part of a triple star system. However, the nature of GJ 113 remains uncertain due to discrepancies in the radial velocity variations observed. We propose two potential explanations for HADS 1's rapid rotation: it could be due to a star engulfing a planet, which transfers angular momentum to the star, or it could be the result of an efficient mechanism that redistributes angular momentum within the star. The presence of g-mode oscillations in HADS 1, which are sensitive to angular momentum redistribution, provides a means to investigate this phenomenon in more detail.

Fake news spreads rapidly and distorts public perception, making it crucial to detect false information. While traditional methods have been effective, they are prone to overfitting due to their reliance on historical data. To counter this issue, we explore the potential of a novel approach that leverages both textual content and emerging audio features to detect false news. Although emerging features provide valuable information, their uniqueness poses significant challenges for a multimodal task. To address this issue, we introduce a new network, called Meta NFP-GNN, that combines neural process priors with meta-learning and graph-based attention mechanisms. This innovative design enables our model to achieve superior performance on multiple datasets, outperforming existing state-of-the-art techniques by a wide margin.

This research paper examines the formation of singularities in periodic solutions to a transport equation, where the equation is given by $\partial_t u + v \partial_x (K(u)) = 0$. Here, K is a non-linear, odd, and non-decreasing function that may have jump discontinuities. We focus on determining how specific properties of the function K influence whether smooth solutions can break down in finite time. In this study, we establish conditions under which initial conditions lead to non-periodic solutions and also result in solutions that are not differentiable. In addition, we explore the impact of non-decreasing and jump discontinuous functions K on solution behavior, including the use of Jensen's formula to analyze convexity. Furthermore, we employ a combination of wave steepening and Taylor's theorem to establish points of loss of differentiability in solutions.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained prominence due to their pivotal role in anti-aliased filter designs for compressed sensing. Building upon Golay complementary matrices, we introduce new types of Golay complementary multi-dimensional arrays, specifically focusing on: (1) GCMF - Golay complementary multi-way arrays and (2) GCMT - Golay complementary tensors. Various construction techniques for GCMF and GCMT are developed and detailed, with an examination of the interconnections between: (1) Golay complementary matrices, (2) Golay complementary multi-way arrays, and (3) Golay complementary tensors.

Quantum tunneling of electrons between energy valleys in silicon's conduction band is used to create non-Abelian symmetry-protected topological states. The absence of valley coupling operators within the same crystallographic plane simplifies the creation of a quantum phase that can be harnessed for computing within the atomic-scale spin-orbitless semiconductors. The absence of coupling allows the formation of intraplane tunneling anomalies. The ability to break conservation laws by introducing an external electric field perpendicular to the plane enables the exchange of spins between electrons and silicon atoms. Theoretical models demonstrate that applying a specific field strength can induce significant changes in the interference patterns observed in the transmission of electrons. The resulting oscillations can reach magnitudes of 100 meV as a function of the position of the atoms, making valley interference an ideal mechanism for exchanging spin information between electrons and silicon atoms within the same plane, free from coupling terms.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting parts are fundamental to a wide range of systems, from social networks to biological ecosystems. Although machine learning models have been successful in predicting the behavior of complex systems, it is challenging to gain a deeper understanding of their underlying dynamics and structure. In this study, we investigate a new type of machine learning model, based on graph neural networks, that can predict the evolution of a class of models known as Markov random walks on large-scale networks. By analyzing this model, we gain valuable insights into the interplay between the network's structure and the walking patterns, and we can even derive a more efficient algorithm to do so. We test this model on synthetic and real-world networks, and it turns out that it can not only accurately predict the model's behavior, but also capture key statistical features of the network and the walking patterns. In addition, we find that the model can uncover a previously unknown transformation, known as a two-step random walk, that significantly influences the network's structure.

We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, establishing relationships among these counts via cumulative sums. These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable us to derive computations related to homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory.

Identifying and locating brain lesions accurately and efficiently is crucial in diagnosing and treating various brain diseases. Current methods for detecting and locating lesions often rely on healthy images and cancerous images, bypassing the need for images with specific types of brain lesions. This research proposes a new method, Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis (PRL-VAE), that can generate a wide range of brain lesions from healthy images alone. PRL-VAE starts with an basic model capable of producing simple lesions, then uses progressive training to develop a more complex synthesis capability. This approach is similar to current advanced techniques that use progressive training to create realistic images and textures. PRL-VAE includes multiple innovations, such as using progressive training to generate a wide range of brain lesions, and employing various evaluation metrics to assess the quality of the generated images. The results show that PRL-VAE can accurately and efficiently synthesize a wide range of brain lesions from healthy images.

GP 2 is a graph-based programming language designed for data mining tasks. It features a compiler that translates programs into an intermediate representation, enabling graph programs to access system resources and access external data. However, GP 2's compiler has limited functionality in translating specific language components, particularly in handling node attributes that reside outside the graph structure. This restriction hampers the GP 2 system's graph representation of programs and necessitates a separate parser for executing programs. In contrast, we present an enhanced version of the GP 2 compiler, which can process node attribute declarations by converting them into Prolog terms and integrating the GP 2 and GP 2 parser into a unified compiler.

Dimensionality reduction techniques like PCA and autoencoders have been widely used in recent years to reduce data dimensions. However, research shows that these methods, in particular PCA, may not be optimal for subsequent machine learning tasks. In response, our group has developed a set of task-oriented feature extraction methods based on contrastive learning that can be applied to various problems, including classification, regression, and time series analysis. This set of methods has been tested on real-world datasets from different domains, encompassing both structured and unstructured data. Our approach has been evaluated using real datasets from UCI, Kaggle, and a medical data set, as well as unstructured data from Hugging Face. Results indicate that our proposed methods, when compared to existing state-of-the-art classification and regression techniques, consistently achieve superior performance across all test cases.

We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs.

Working with categorical data is now common in many applications, and for models that include such data, sparse and可解释性 regularization methods are highly sought after.  Despite its usefulness for model selection, RARE has mainly been developed for individual variables, and its group-level counterpart has not been thoroughly investigated.  This paper aims to investigate the RARE counterpart for a specific group of variables, and we also propose a novel algorithm to efficiently solve the resulting optimization problem. Through numerical experiments and comparison with existing methods, we demonstrate the effectiveness of LG RARE in achieving faster convergence, better convergence stability, and superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and variable selection capability.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved significant success in natural language tasks, but their reliance on training data makes them prone to incorporating biases and making factual errors. To address these limitations, traditional methods such as knowledge graphs and rule-based systems have been used to enhance the interpretability and accuracy of NLP models through structure prior. However, current structured methods struggle to effectively capture the complex patterns present in large language models. To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel structured input format called LLM-Specific Knowledge (SK), which includes simple entity descriptions, nuanced relational statements, and context-aware question embeddings. We further develop a tailored attention infusion module that enables the model to effectively integrate LLM-Specific Knowledge and significantly boosts performance on various benchmark datasets while reducing hallucinations and improving factual accuracy.

Achieving high-quality line joins in mobile data visualization applications poses a significant challenge due to anti-aliasing effects caused by rounding errors during pixel coordinate conversions. These artifacts can severely compromise the visual appeal of vector maps, particularly when depicting geographic features such as rivers, roads, and coastlines. Existing solutions for smoothing effects often involve computationally intensive algorithms, which are impractical for real-time rendering on mobile devices. In this study, a novel approach is proposed to calculate line joins efficiently with enhanced visual quality. This technique utilizes high-precision approximations of $\pi$ to produce a more accurate and visually pleasing result, which outperforms current methods in both performance and anti-aliasing effects. Our approach is demonstrated to be 10 times faster than current leading techniques, providing a substantial improvement in the real-time rendering of vector maps on mobile devices.

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed, dividing the input into short and long sequences for distinct RNN models. Building upon this concept, a dual-path RNN was further developed to perform single speech enhancement by processing short and long sequences through separate forward and backward RNN components. The model's output fusion is guided by a dynamic convolution layer, and an adaptive batch normalization method was applied to expedite training and boost performance. The resulting network can be fine-tuned from a dual-path RNN model's weights, significantly reducing the need for data and hyperparameter optimization. Experiments on the NVIDIA Multi-Speaker Noisy Text Telephone (NST-T) dataset showed that the initial dual-LSTM RNN and fine-tuned single RNN models outperformed the baseline MEMS model, achieving lower weighted SDR improvements of 1.62, 1.51, and 1.49 dB, respectively.

Recently, multi-fluid models have shown promise in improving the prediction of atmospheric convection within weather and climate systems. To develop such models with just two fluids as a simpler alternative, we need to create more straightforward multi-fluid convection parameters. A Rayleigh-Benard convection simulator has been developed in a single-column model framework to serve as an accurate testbed for such parameters. This paper presents a two-fluid Rayleigh-Benard convection model that can be accurately compared with the simulator, and we have evaluated several existing and proposed two-fluid convection parameters. We found that the existing Mass Flux Free Convection parameter and a novel mass flux parameter with separate convective and entrainment fluxes for both fluids delivered the most accurate predictions with minimal tuning, and are thus recommended for use in multi-fluid models.

We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with each system comprising an atom and a mode of the electromagnetic field. In this study, we analyze the spread of entanglement within the system's degrees of freedom. Interestingly, under certain conditions, entanglement is found exclusively in the electromagnetic modes and or within the atomic system, while under other conditions, it is present in both components. Furthermore, we are able to distinguish between atomic and mode entanglement that was found to be genuinely multipartite in our research. We also investigate the amount of correlations needed among the atoms to create atomic entanglement, as well as the impact of atomic and mode entanglement on the system's overall behavior.

Social media platforms, particularly Twitter, have become significant sources
of information about public sentiment. This study presents a method for
determining the emotional content of Tweets using deep learning techniques.
Our approach leverages the ability of Recurrent Neural Networks, specifically
LSTM networks, to effectively handle sequential data and capture long-term
dependencies. A classifier based on an LSTM network was developed to predict
the positive or negative sentiment of a given Tweet. This model was trained
and tested on a dataset of labeled Tweets, and its performance was compared
to that of other traditional machine learning methods. Our results show that
our proposed deep learning approach achieves high accuracy in predicting
Twitter sentiment.

For this study, we examined the shadow cast by non-linear charged AdS black holes in the context of a cubic quasi-local electromagnetic model. We analyzed how parameters related to this model, as well as specific charges and angular velocity, influence the shadow pattern. Our research reveals that the quasi-local nature of the cubic model leads to distinct differences compared to the Reissner-Nordstrom AdS model, particularly in how it affects shadow behavior beyond a certain threshold of specific charge. Our study also shows that the black hole's specific charge has an inverse relationship with the size of the shadow, whereas angular velocity is directly proportional to the shadow's size. Our results further indicate that the dark matter parameter influences the shadow pattern in an inversely proportional manner.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated by the vast size of its Hilbert space. Multiple techniques have been developed to create graphical representations of density operators using tomograms, which are directly linked to the underlying state through a specific transformation. This paper focuses on analyzing two distinct phenomena - quantum synchronization and the deterioration of entanglement - in the continuous variable systems by examining their corresponding effects on the associated tomograms. We demonstrate how the disappearance of entanglement in the Duan criterion manifests as a change in the tomogram's structure, whereas the onset of quantum synchronization results in a specific pattern within the tomogram that can be described by Bessel functions.

360-degree streaming videos can offer immersive experiences, but their full potential is hindered by high bandwidth requirements. To address this, viewport prediction technology aims to enhance streaming efficiency by pre-loading the area around a user's focus. To develop a more effective prediction algorithm, it's crucial to gather data that reflects real-world interactions. This paper introduces a new dataset consisting of subtitles and corresponding pre-requests from a real 360-degree virtual tourism video. Furthermore, the paper proposes a subtitle-driven prediction method that leverages textual information to enhance the accuracy of viewport prediction, effectively identifying the pre-request field of view.

Tensor network methods have been widely used in non-equilibrium problems involving 1D systems with a finite temperature. Although these methods are efficient in representing certain low-entropy states within the thermal density matrix, they are not as effective when considering the thermal state in the grand canonical ensemble. In this context, an excessive number of canonical degrees of freedom must be managed, significantly increasing the number of parameters required. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes a combination of thermal superblocks and isometries to directly represent the thermal state in the bosonic or fermionic grand canonical ensemble. This new algorithm ensures that each partition of the system can be described using a two-dimensional slice within an enlarged Hilbert space, thereby ensuring that the total entropy is accurately captured. Moreover, this new method also ensures that the system's thermalization dynamics, when simulated using Heisenberg dynamics for local observables, are captured with high accuracy. Notably, this level of precision is comparable to that achieved using a tDMRG calculation in a significantly larger system in the canonical ensemble, and it is accomplished without incurring an excessive number of canonical degrees of freedom.

We establish that for any given probability distribution on the line line, random variables limited in how much they can individually affect outcomes (called (a,b)-decouplable) can be effectively replaced by variables with limited variation, specifically, that are squared-bounded, within a certain error margin. This margin is determined by a factor and the probability distribution's characteristics, specifically, that lack of extreme values and a certain level of "spread out" behavior. This result can be used to achieve better understanding and techniques in various statistical and machine learning contexts, such as when analyzing sums of functions, estimating complex functions, and managing functions of multiple variables.

The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's variance is being quantified, and calculations show that non-linear small-x saturation corrections stem from this impact in the low-x TMD PDF.

Researchers have developed a new concept for a highly compact device known as a unidirectional magnetophotonic surface crystal switch, which uses the significant magnetic properties of half-Hamaker metals to control light transmission at specific frequencies. By manipulating these magnetic properties with electric currents, they demonstrated surface crystal routing, switching, and gating capabilities, leading to a proof of concept for a surface crystal gate that can control a 50nm transistor. This research highlights the importance of advanced magnetic materials in nanophotonic integration and miniaturization, with potential applications in high-speed, low-power, and compact photonic devices.

Knowledge distillation is a technique used to enable small neural networks to replicate the performance of larger networks. Traditionally, this process involves using data from the larger network to train the smaller one. However, this process can be time-consuming and computationally expensive. This paper presents a novel approach that allows for knowledge from black-box decision-based models to be transferred to parametric models, even when there is no access to their internal data. This decision-based distiling approach is unique as it is neither similar to log-based nor example-based methods. This approach makes no assumptions about the target model and is especially beneficial in scenarios where retraining is costly. This paper evaluates the performance of two decision-based knowledge distillation algorithms, one using only the predictions of the target model and another that also incorporates predictions from a white-box model as a starting point. This paper's results indicate that decision-based knowledge from neural models can effectively enhance model performance, with significant improvements observed when the size of the target model is considerably larger than the model.

Researchers have identified the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay for the first time, and they've also found supporting evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay. To quantify the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0_S$ branching fraction, it is estimated to be between $3.4$ and $6.5 \times 10^{-6}$, with an uncertainty of $\pm 1.0 \times 10^{-6}$. The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^{*0}$ decay branching fraction is estimated to be between $0.6$ and $2.4 \times 10^{-6}$, with an uncertainty of $\pm 0.6 \times 10^{-6}$.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. However, for specific modules, particularly those that are direct sums of irreducible modules with distinct components, the submodule lattice can be more easily determined. Given an expression of a module M as a direct sum of irreducible modules F_i, where each F_i appears only once, we aim to construct the lattice of its submodules using information about the submodule lattice of the direct sum of these irreducible components. This approach involves mapping each lattice with its join and meet operations and utilizing a specific functor that preserves the lattice structure. This paper will walk through the process of applying this approach to several examples.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly boosted by incorporating imitation learning, which leverages expert demonstrations to guide an agent. However, accessing expert demonstrations often proves costly and impractical in real-world scenarios. This study Co-Imitation Learning explores a novel approach where agents learn from peers to guide one another in a population. Co-Imitation Learning utilizes peer data without the need for explicit demonstrations, leading to a unique policy update rule that balances the benefits of peer data with the incentives of reinforcement learning. The proposed method is validated through comprehensive experiments on Markov Decision Processes and Large-Scale Robot Navigation, revealing its effectiveness in improving performance and reducing the necessity for expert demonstrations.

This paper provides a metric comparison between two codex frameworks, 
including one originally proposed by P. A. Chou, and a new variation of that 
framework we developed. We calculate the PAC functions for the codes in question, 
achieve a computed free distance of 14 for the 384-bit Golay code utilizing our 
PAC construction with modulation, and determine the optimal free distance of 
10 among all possible codex formulations that incorporate the PAC as a component.

Using reinforcement learning post maximum likelihood estimation pre-training can substantially enhance neural machine translation efficiency. Nonetheless, a significant limitation of RL for NMT applications is its reliance on binary action spaces, which constrains the model's learning potential. We investigate a non-stationary multi-action space setting for RL in neural machine translation, which involves simultaneously managing multiple distinct action distributions that change over time. We develop a novel algorithm, Reinforcement Learning with Multi-action Space, to effectively handle this scenario. Computational efficiency is maintained through parameter sharing, while performance is boosted by dynamically adjusting shared parameters. Our method achieves notable improvements over traditional RL with action space, yielding a 1.5 to 5.5 BLEU score gain on diverse datasets.

The study of quantum systems under periodic influence is highly relevant to
current research and applications in the field of quantum technology.
Despite being influenced by time-varying conditions, many systems reach a
special state of stability known as a periodically driven non-equilibrium
steady state, featuring unique properties. This study presents direct
measurements of such a state in a semiconductor spin qubit, utilizing an
oscillating magnetic field. As the intensity of this field increases, the
system gradually transitions from a large to a small effective driving
environment, exhibiting distinct dynamics and influence from internal
interactions. The study's findings show that the time-driven properties
disappear in a driven-non-equilibrium steady state, with theoretical and
experimental findings aligning with each other.

We explore how several established recurrent operators, including curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators, can be utilized to demonstrate the existence of biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space that are not minimal. Furthermore, we provide proof of the minimality of specific recurrent hypersurfaces, including the sphere and Cayley plane, and establish original minimality theorems for sphere and Cayley plane hypersurfaces that are biharmonic and employ particular recurrent operators. These conclusions are presented as distinct propositions and corollaries.

A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words in N^k can be classified as p/q-recognisable if a specific condition is met: the set of words whose values in base p/q belong to a given subset R^k of (p/q)^k can be determined by a finite automaton that processes words in N^k in colexicographic order. This paper investigates the properties of r^k-recognisable sets for different values of r greater than 1, and it is demonstrated that for a rational r greater than 1, r^k-recognisable subsets of (r^k)^k correspond precisely to semi-linear sets. Additionally, the set of recognisable subsets of (r^k)^k is found to be finite.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that enables applications to implement atomic transactions across multiple documents or nodes. Although general tailable cursors in MongoDB have been found to be inconsistent under transactions, this issue can be addressed with a straightforward consistency model known as read your writes. This paper presents a formal framework for analyzing the transactional behavior of MongoDB, including a specification of its transactions, and subsequently, through this framework, provides consistent consistency checks for the "read your writes" scenario. Initial results show that MongoDB adheres to atomic transactions but has been found to violate read your writes in case of regular cursor operations. This situation can be addressed by avoiding certain types of reads, for instance, by not reading data from other collections or by using transactions with a short duration.

Using the elementary symmetric function basis, we re-express the chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths with a bounce number of three via a combinatorial interpretation related to the inverse of the Kostka matrix from Egecioglu and Remmel's work on its combinatorial properties. By a known reduction, this re-expression also applies to Dyck paths with a bounce number of three when considering their associated semigroup permutations. A chromatic poset framework was originally established by Garsia and Remmel in 1991, with a simpler, more intuitive version being presented here. This re-expression can be extended to a broader class of permutation-defined posets through the application of Egecioglu and Remmel's E-positive combinatorial approach based on Eulerian polynomials. A specific example is provided to demonstrate this extended class of posets.

Research on intricate networks has uncovered a concealed structural aspect that significantly influences network dynamics and processes occurring within them. To investigate these network dynamics in relation to their underlying geometry, a model was developed to represent triangular network assemblies consisting of triangles and edges, where spins can exist in two states: ferromagnetic triangles and ferroelectric edges. As this model undergoes a specific parameter transformation, it experiences a ferromagnetic-ferroelectric phase transition accompanied by a distinct change in magnetization dynamics, mirroring a second-order Griffiths phase transition observed in random bipartite networks with triangle-based connectivity. Monte Carlo simulations reveal that this triangle-based connectivity results in unique triangle flipping during the ferromagnetic-ferroelectric transition, providing evidence of a hidden geometry's influence on phase transitions and offering a novel perspective on the relationship between network structure and the emergence of complex behavior.

We present new, direct measurements of solar wind energy flux close to the
inner edge of the heliosphere, obtained using data from the Parker Solar
Probe. As the first such assessments, this analysis of 149 days of data, from
0.21 to 0.29 astronomical units, reveals solar wind energy flux values
ranging from 0.1 to 100 Watts per square meter, with an average of 3.92 Watts
per square meter. Our findings show that this energy flux is influenced by
proximity to the Sun, previous encounters with slow solar wind streams, and
high-speed streams near the Sun, and we discuss the implications of these
discoveries for understanding radiation near the Sun and for future space
exploration.

Realease Emotion recognition has become an established field, yet it still poses significant difficulties, especially when it comes to accurately identifying emotions in spoken language. This challenge is exacerbated by the frequent discrepancy between the characteristics of speech in laboratory settings and those in real-life situations. This disparity is particularly pronounced when it comes to speech recorded in real-world situations with diverse speech qualities and listener experiences. This paper presents a novel approach that leverages deep reinforcement learning to adapt models from high-quality training data to more complex and varied recorded speech, achieving superior results compared to conventional adaptation methods. This approach allows for efficient adaptation to new recorded speech with limited access to the original model's parameters. This has been demonstrated in multiple scenarios with varied speech recorded situations, showcasing improved accuracy in diverse recorded situations with significant reductions in adaptation costs when the model's parameter space is restricted.

Researchers studying strong shock waves in an expanding universe have found that their findings hold true for various, more complex initial conditions. When a spherical void is embedded within an uniformly expanding universe and filled with gas, the pressure and velocity behind a spherical shock wave's front have been observed to match previously derived scaling laws. This agreement remains valid even as the expansion rate gradually declines over time.

Using 3.8 inverse femtobarns of data collected by the LHCb detector, researchers have examined the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ decay process and investigated its differential decay rate structure. By analyzing the angular position of the $D_s^{*-}$ particle within this decay chain, they have determined key parameters that describe this decay rate's behavior. These parameters are found to be $\Gamma_{1}=\Gamma_{0}\times (1.00\pm 0.04\pm 0.02\pm 0.04)$, $\alpha= -0.56\pm 0.13\pm 0.05\pm 0.07$, and $\omega= 0$. The symbols $\Gamma_{1}$, $\alpha$, and $\omega$ represent form factors relevant to this analysis. The results obtained from this angular analysis are then applied to evaluate the consistency of previously reported form factor values.

A recent study classifies Schr\"odinger operators with periodic coefficients, leading to operators with generalized Hermite polynomials as part of their spectral structure. These results build on a 1931 work by Bloch, together with an anisotropy-free condition, resulting in operators that are structurally identical to generalized Hermite polynomials. This classification, defined through linear differential operators, facilitates the identification of periodic Schr\"odinger operators based on their spectrum, with the standard Hermite polynomials corresponding to trigonometrically periodic operators and discrete spectrum case. The study also establishes that the two-degree-of-liberty Heisenberg algebra arises from periodic Schr\"odinger operators, with the standard and generalized Hermite polynomials occupying distinct degree classes within the algebra.

A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolving how to objectively identify patterns in autocorrelation functions that indicate the presence or absence of underlying structure. In this study, we develop and apply linear and non-linear filtering techniques to analyze the self-similar structure of the acoustic emissions generated during the sudden releases of elastic energy in the peeling process of adhesive tape. Our results reveal that, despite its initial apparent randomness, this noise exhibits a distinct three-component structure when examining short, medium, and long time lags. Furthermore, we find that basic filtering methods successfully isolate the self-similar behavior that characterizes the elastic energy releases at various scales.
The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed, with an investigation of thermal behavior and the transformation of non-abelian aether-like terms under (finite) temperature conditions.

This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established before deriving the Hedging Variance process, which enables the estimation of the expected unit hedging cost based on initial inputs. Initially, discrete-time analysis was conducted with applications primarily in the determination of minimum capital requirements for options sold by financial institutions. To achieve this, a Quasi-Reverse Hamiltonian Jacobi (QRHJ) differential equation is established, which, in continuous time, provides a more accurate and broadly applicable solution. This equation's solution yields closed-form solutions for variance processes, providing a more accurate and broadly applicable solution.

A new job or business opportunity can significantly impact an individual's family and even subsequent generations. In the ever-changing job market and economic landscape, allocating access to new opportunities between generations requires taking into account multiple generations' incentives and dynamics. A dynamic model of intergenerational mobility investigates multiple generations' incentives in a two-period setting, where past mobility shapes past human capital, affecting future generations. The paper explores the complex relationship between generations, where past generations' achievements can both disadvantage future generations through relative deprivation and give them a sense of gratitude. The model can capture various forms of intergenerational mobility, from nepotism to affirmative action, grand reciprocity, and grand guilt. The paper also examines the model's ability to capture dynamics that simpler, two-generation models cannot.

In 2015, CERN's LINAC4 to LHC at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) upgrade pathway project initiated a series of novel beam tests at the LHC. These tests, which are set to continue with the LHC's upgraded capacity, involved injecting higher intensity beams and scanning various luminosity profiles across the machine's circumference. The primary goal of these luminosity scans was to measure the dimensions of the proton beams using the pattern of collisions induced by beam–gas interactions and particle collisions. This paper presents the data from these scans, processed using the ALICE detector, and provides an in-depth analysis of the information gathered.

This paper explores the optimization of a strongly convex objective function 
across a network, which may be governed by the consensus algorithm. 
We focus on robustness in decentralized optimization, specifically in the context 
of malicious attacks on the communication links between nodes. 
We propose an optimized, distributed algorithm that achieves a convex objective 
through the exchange of quantized data. 
We also investigate the impact of malicious attacks on the network, focusing on 
both node and communication link attacks. 
We derive convergence rates for our algorithm under these attack scenarios and 
obtain performance bounds for both strongly convex and convex objective functions. 
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through numerical simulations.

The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, this study's impact is significantly limited by the complexity of the instrumentation and data processing methods of modern experiments, which are highly sophisticated and involve multiple components and algorithms. A notorious issue is that subtle and non-obvious systematic effects of the instrumentation can masquerade as and outshine the faint cosmic signal. Consequently, these systematics must be carefully measured and accounted for in order to accurately interpret the data. This is particularly challenging as they can be difficult to replicate and model due to their unique nature. In our study, we aim to replicate the Planck and S4 polarimetry instruments' systematic effects in order to accurately test the robustness of the methods designed to detect the cosmic linear polarisation. In order to do this, we have developed a flexible framework that allows for the replication of a wide range of instrumental and data processing related effects. In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful sequence, prior approaches rely on either linear models or models based on attention mechanisms, but they fail to replicate human performance and don't utilize potential language understanding. This paper investigates whether a powerful pre-trained sequence model like BART can effectively solve this problem by examining its performance and internal components. Our research reveals that BART achieves top performance, matching human levels of accuracy, and that its different modules play distinct roles in the sequence ordering process. Furthermore, we identify sequence-aware features that can enhance models for this task and make our dataset and findings available to the community.

The rapid spread of deepfake technology on social media poses a significant risk to public trust, necessitating the development of efficient and scalable countermeasures. Despite advancements in generative models, current deepfake detection techniques struggle to effectively generalize across various generative methods due to their heavy reliance on pattern-specific features. In this study, we introduce the MD-CSDNetwork, a novel multi-domain detection framework built upon separate sensory encoding branches for real and fake images. By applying network stitching techniques to the respective image frequency domains, the MD-CSDNetwork successfully combines high-level semantic information with subtle artifact information, resulting in enhanced feature representation. Empirical evaluations on the Deepfake Detection Challenge (DFDC) dataset demonstrate the superiority of our approach over existing methods, with performance metrics including an F1 score of 90.1, an AUPR of 94.1, and generalization capabilities across multiple detection checkpoints.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, research into these problems was taken up by various scholars including F. A. Valentine, A. D. Alexandrov, and T. C. Kuppner, each contributing solutions to one of Menger's problems or exploring the angle function within the context of specific spaces. This paper introduces a distinct definition for the abstract angle function, which, according to a recent approach, results in the previously mentioned problems no longer being applicable.
